text.p: Croatians vote on Sunday to elect a president for the second time since they gained independence from communist Yugoslavia in 1991.
Following are the key facts about Croatia:
POPULATION: 4.78 million (State Statistics Bureau 1995 estimate).

There has been no census since 1991 because of the war in former Yugoslavia. However the last census split the population as follows: 3.7 million Croatians, 580,000 Serbs, 43,500 Moslems and 113,000 others (Slovenes, Italians, Czechs, Albanians, Montenegrins, Gypsies, Macedonians, Ruthenians). Some 100,000 people declared themselves as Yugoslavs and more than 73,000 declined to declare their nationality.
Government estimates show some 135,000 ethnic Serbs left Croatia in 1995, after their rebellion was crushed, settling in neighbouring Yugoslavia and Serb-held Bosnia.
Up to 50,000 found refuge in Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb enclave in Croatia, but the exact figure is unknown. Around 17,000 Serbs have returned to their pre-war homes in Croatia.
According to latest government statistics, there are 105,000 Bosnian refugees in Croatia.

AREA: 56,538 sq km (21,829 sq miles). Territorial waters 31,900 sq km (12,316 sq miles). The Adriatic coastline, which includes 1,185 islands, islets and reefs, is 5,740 km (3,566 miles) long and famed for its clear waters.
Croatia is bordered by Slovenia in the north, Hungary in the northeast, Serbia in the east, Bosnia and Herzegovina in the south and Montenegro in the southeast.
CAPITAL: Zagreb, population 867,865.
LANGUAGE: The official language is Croatian, written in Roman script.
RELIGION: (1991 census) Roman Catholics 77 percent, Orthodox 11.0 percent, Moslem 1.1 percent and 633 Jews (0.01 percent). Remainder includes Greek Catholics, Protestants, atheists and others.

ECONOMY: Croatia is negotiating admission to the World Trade Organisation and the Central European Free Trade Organisation (CEFTA) with member countries. It is not likely to be in the first wave of post-communist countries to join the European Union.
Three international rating agencies gave Croatia investment grade ratings of BBB- and equivalent in January 1997. Standard and Poor's placed it just behind Poland and ahead of Slovakia and Greece.
An austerity programme introduced in 1993 curbed inflation which was running at 38 percent a month. In 1996 it was 3.5 percent. The government expects it to remain below 5.0 percent this year.
Croatia's GDP is officially expected to grow by five to six percent in 1997, IMF estimates GDP rose by five percent in 96.
In 1995 industry accounted for 20 percent of GDP, public sector services 24 percent, agriculture 11 percent, trade 8 percent and tourism 4-5 percent.
Unemployment eased slightly to 16.6 percent in April 1997 from 16.7 percent in March.

HISTORY: After the last Croatian king died at the end of the 11th century, Croatians elected Hungarian King Koloman as their ruler in 1102. Faced with conquering Turkish troops they turned to the Habsburg monarchy for help and eventually fell under Austria's direct military rule in 1671.

Austro-Hungarian rule ended in 1918 when Croatia become part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. The country was officially renamed Yugoslavia after Serbian King Alexander proclaimed a dictatorship in 1929.

Yugoslavia joined the fascist countries in the Tripartite Pact in March 1941 but withdrew after a military coup. Two weeks later Germany bombarded Belgrade and Yugoslavia capitulated within a few days. In April 1941 Ante Pavelic, founder of the Ustasha Movement, proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia (NDH). It became Germany's ally, persecuting Jews, Serbs, Gypsies and Croatian communists.

Many Croats sided with an anti-fascist partisan movement led by communist Josip Broz Tito. With the aid of the Western Allies, the Communist party took power in 1945 and formed the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with Tito as president. Croatia was one of the six federal republics.

Following Tito's death in May 1980 federal Yugoslavia began to crumble. In April 1990, the Croatian Democratic Union and its leader Franjo Tudjman, formerly Tito's general, won the first multi-party elections since World War Two. On May 30 the new Croatian parliament was formally established.

On June 25, 1991 Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia. But the Serb minority opposed its secession and started a rebellion, backed by the Serbian-led Yugoslav army. By January 1992, when a U.N. ceasefire was agreed, one-third of Croatia was under the control of the Serbs, who proclaimed their own republic of Krajina comprising three enclaves.

Croatia was formally recognised by the European Community on January 15, 1992 and became a U.N. member in May 1992. In August 1992 Tudjman was elected president and his HDZ party won an absolute majority in the Lower House of Parliament.

In two blitz offensives in May and August 1995, the Croatian army reconquered the largest chunks of the Krajina, prompting an exodus of Serbs. In November 1995 Zagreb agreed to reintegrate peacefully the last Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, after a transitional United Nations administration, whose mandate expires next month.
In December 1995, together with Bosnia and Serbia, Croatia signed the Dayton peace agreement, committing itself to a permanent ceasefire and the return of all refugees.

The ruling HDZ party continued to dominate by winning the October 1995 elections for parliament's lower house and the April 1997 vote for the upper house of parliament and local administrative bodies.
